title: Before Applying to an Affiliate Program: Prepare a Webmaster Readiness File
description: Prepare a clear affiliate-program application by documenting your site, audience, traffic sources, promotional methods and compliance processes before applying.
excerpt: A practical application-readiness checklist for webmasters who want to explain how their site works and verify program requirements before sending traffic.
keyTakeaways: Describe your site, audience and promotional placements specifically rather than relying on broad claims.
Document each traffic source and promotional method so you can compare them with program rules.
Check the application’s information requirements and ask about ambiguous restrictions before launching links.
Use accurate, supportable statements about your site and do not imply permissions, results or relationships you do not have.
Keep a copy of submitted answers and the version of the program terms you reviewed.

sections.heading: Build a factual description of your site
paragraphs: A useful application begins with a concise, accurate account of what your site publishes and who it serves. Explain the site’s topic, main content formats, language and the pages where a potential referral link would appear. Avoid generic descriptions that make it difficult for a program reviewer to understand the visitor journey. If your site is new, say so and describe what is already live rather than implying an established audience or history.

Support each statement with evidence you can provide if asked, such as live page examples, an editorial policy or a description of your publishing schedule. Do not invent visitor numbers, conversion results or audience characteristics. If an application asks for metrics you do not have, clarify that fact rather than estimating. A credible description is more useful than inflated claims because it lets both sides assess whether the site and offer are a sensible operational fit.
bullets: List the site’s live sections and the formats you publish.
Describe the audience in terms supported by your content, not assumptions about individual visitors.
Identify where links would appear and what context would surround them.
Mark unmeasured or unavailable metrics as unknown.

sections.heading: Map your traffic and promotion methods
paragraphs: Programs can set different rules for search traffic, paid advertising, email, social media, coupons, redirects or other promotional methods. Do not assume a method is permitted because it is common elsewhere. Make a source-by-source map of how visitors reach your site and how you plan to direct them to a program. Include owned pages, paid placements and any third-party distribution you control or commission. This gives you a concrete way to compare your operation with the program’s written restrictions.

When a rule is unclear, ask a narrow question before using that traffic source. For example, identify the channel, placement and type of link involved, then request the program’s interpretation in writing. Keep the reply with your application records. A general approval to join should not be treated as permission for every later campaign or traffic method, especially if the terms distinguish between channels or require separate review.

sections.heading: Review program restrictions before describing your plan
paragraphs: Application readiness is not legal advice, and a program’s approval does not replace your own responsibilities. Applicable disclosure and advertising rules can depend on location and circumstances. Identify the obligations that apply to your publishing operation and seek qualified guidance when needed. Keep disclosures clear to visitors and ensure they match the actual commercial relationship.

sections.heading: Explain how you will manage links and visitor expectations
paragraphs: A reviewer should be able to understand what a visitor sees before clicking and where the link leads. Describe whether the link appears in an editorial comparison, a resource page, an email or another placement. Explain how you keep labels and disclosures clear, and how you check that a destination remains relevant to the page. Avoid promising a visitor a benefit, price or outcome unless you can substantiate it and the program permits that claim.

Outline basic link operations: who creates links, how campaigns are tagged, how redirects are checked and how broken or changed destinations are handled. If you plan to use tracking identifiers, describe the system at a high level without overstating what it measures. A simple, documented process is more persuasive than claiming sophisticated tracking you do not actually operate. If creative materials require approval, include the review step and do not publish unapproved material while awaiting a decision.
bullets: Show the visitor context for each proposed link placement.
State where commercial disclosures will appear.
Describe how you verify destinations and remove outdated links.
Identify who checks creative approval and program-term changes.

sections.heading: Submit, record and reassess the application
paragraphs: Before submission, check that your site is accessible, the pages you cite are live and the answers are consistent with one another. Save a dated copy of the application, submitted supporting materials and the program terms you reviewed. If the program asks for clarification, respond with specific facts and update your own notes. Do not interpret silence, a pending application or account access as approval for a promotional method that the terms require you to obtain separately.

After acceptance, compare the final account settings and current program terms with your application plan. Record any conditions, limits or required approvals. Recheck the rules before changing traffic sources, adding paid promotion or introducing a new placement. If your site or ownership changes, review whether the application information remains accurate. This turns a one-time form into a small governance workflow and makes it easier to explain decisions if questions arise.
bullets: Save dated copies of terms, application answers and written clarifications.
Track unresolved restrictions and do not treat them as approved.
Review the plan whenever you add a traffic channel or change a site section.
Assign responsibility for checking updates and maintaining link disclosures.

faqs.question: What if an affiliate application asks for traffic figures I do not have?
faqs.answer: Do not invent a number. State that the figure is unavailable, provide only metrics you can support, and describe your current site and planned promotion accurately. If the form requires a figure, ask the program how it wants a new or unmeasured site to answer.

faqs.question: Does approval to join automatically approve every traffic source?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Program rules may restrict particular channels or require separate review. Read the terms and obtain written clarification for methods that are unclear before using them.

faqs.question: What should I save after applying?
faqs.answer: Keep a dated copy of your application, the terms you reviewed, supporting materials and written answers from the program. These records help you compare later decisions with the information available when you applied.

faqs.question: Should I wait for acceptance before publishing affiliate links?
faqs.answer: Follow the program’s stated application and approval process. Do not assume that a submitted application, pending status or ability to create a link means you are authorized to use it. Check the specific terms and any required approvals.
